q: How does the FOM define an ETOPS operation in terms of distance from an adequate airport?
a: A flight that operates over a route containing a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air.

src.quote: flights that operate over a route that contains a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air
src.note: This 60-minute threshold is the trigger for ETOPS. On the 787 fleet, the ICAO-equivalent term is EDTO. The one-engine-inoperative cruise speed used to measure the 60 minutes is the 787's .84M/290 KIAS.

q: What distance defines an Extended Over-Water Operation?
a: An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline.

src.quote: An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline.
src.note: Do not confuse the 50 NM over-water trigger with the 60-minute ETOPS trigger; they are separate concepts.

q: What is the two-part premise of ETOPS philosophy?
a: To preclude a diversion and, if one were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion.

src.ref: FOM 6.1.3 — ETOPS Philosophy: Preclude and Protect
src.quote: The premise of ETOPS is to preclude a diversion and, if it were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion.
src.note: Preclude layers include design, testing, maintenance, and flight ops procedures; protect layers include monitored alternates, enhanced comms, and enhanced dispatch fuel.

q: For an adequate airport, within what portion of runway length must a turbojet be able to stop, and from what height?
a: Within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway, measured from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway.

src.quote: Turbojet aircraft must be able to be stopped within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway.
src.note: An adequate airport must also meet 14 CFR 121.197 landing limitations and Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF), or be an active military airport.

q: What minimum rescue and firefighting (RFFS) category must each designated ETOPS alternate airport have?
a: RFFS equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher.

src.quote: rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher
src.note: Note the distinction: an adequate airport does not require ARFF, but a designated ETOPS alternate must have at least ICAO Category 4 RFFS.

q: What firefighting response time must an FAA-approved ETOPS alternate meet, and what does it actually require?
a: A 30-minute response time. It does not require equipment to be pre-positioned; it means firefighting equipment must be available on arrival of the diverting airplane and remain on station as long as needed.

src.quote: firefighting assistance within a 30-minute response time
src.note: The FOM clarifies the 30-minute response time means equipment available on arrival of the diverting airplane, not standing by for 30 minutes beforehand.

q: What is Alaska Airlines' authorized Maximum Diversion Time (MDT), and where does the ETOPS area of operation begin?
a: The authorized MDT is 180 minutes. The ETOPS area of operation begins beyond 60 minutes from the adequate airport and extends to the planned MDT from the planned ETOPS alternates.

src.quote: The Alaska Airlines' authorized MDT is 180 minutes.
src.note: MDT is computed at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air, and the MDT the flight was planned on must be listed in the Dispatch Release.

q: For ETOPS up to and including 180 minutes, the time to an ETOPS alternate may not exceed what limit?
a: It may not exceed the approved time for the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the most limiting fire-suppression system time for compartments required to have fire suppression) minus 15 minutes.

src.quote: would exceed the approved time for the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the aircraft's most limiting fire-suppression system time for those cargo and baggage compartments required by regulation to have fire-suppression systems) minus 15 minutes
src.note: This 'minus 15 minutes' buffer also appears in 6.2.5 as the ceiling on actual diversion time per 14 CFR 121.633.

q: What can occasionally reduce the MDT to 120 minutes, and what is the maximum diversion time to an ETOPS alternate from any point along the route?
a: MEL-deferred items may occasionally limit the MDT to 120 minutes. The diversion time from any point along the route must be no more than 120 or 180 minutes (as dispatched) to the ETOPS alternate.

src.quote: Occasionally, MEL-deferred items may limit the MDT to 120 minutes.
src.note: This diversion time is measured at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air and yields a fixed Maximum Diversion Distance (MDD) per aircraft.

q: For the 787, what single-engine speed and what flying distances correspond to the 60-, 120-, and 180-minute rings?
a: 787: .84M/290 KIAS, giving 410 nm at 60 minutes, 806 nm at 120 minutes, and 1207 nm at 180 minutes.

src.ref: FOM 6.2.3 — Table 6.2.3(1): ETOPS Area of Operations
src.note: These are the fixed 787 distances that define the range rings; the 60-minute ring (410 nm) marks the EEP/EXP distance.

q: What are the three critical fuel scenarios used to compute fuel to fly to an ETOPS alternate?
a: (1) Immediate descent from cruise to 10,000 ft with both engines operating (pressurization loss); (2) descent to best single-engine altitude with one engine operating (engine failure); (3) immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (simultaneous pressurization loss and engine failure).

src.quote: An immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (pressurization loss and simultaneous engine-failure scenario)
src.note: The fuel calculation uses the most critical of these scenarios from the critical point (CP/ETP) to the diversion airport.

q: Upon reaching the ETOPS alternate, what fuel allowance does the critical fuel calculation include?
a: Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing.

src.quote: Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing.
src.note: This arrival allowance is one element added on top of the fuel to fly to the alternate under the critical scenario.

q: How is forecast wind adjusted in the ETOPS critical fuel calculation?
a: Forecast wind speeds are increased by 5%, resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind.

src.quote: forecast wind speeds which have been increased by 5% (resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind)
src.note: This is one of several conservative adjustments, alongside icing, engine deterioration, APU use, and MEL/CDL penalties.

q: What does the '(AS) ER or ETOPS' designation mean in the MEL, and how is it typically used?
a: It refers to Extended Operations of a two-engine aircraft with a type design approval for ETOPS. The designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item.

src.quote: The ER or ETOPS designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item.
src.note: MEL ETOPS-critical items may limit the ETOPS area of operations or preclude ETOPS entirely; compliance with the MEL is a critical factor in ETOPS.

q: For the 787, what one-engine-inoperative reference speed, reference weight, and reference flight level are used to derive ETOPS speeds?
a: 787: .84M/290 KIAS, a reference weight of 515,000 lb, and reference FL350.

src.note: Reference weights and OEI flight levels derive the ring distances; for dispatch planning, actual planned weights are used.

q: How long does the ETOPS Dispatch Release / Pre-Departure Check remain valid, and what is required after that?
a: It remains valid for four hours after the scheduled departure time. After the release expiration, a new Pre-Departure Check and an amended Dispatch Release are required.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.2 — Flight Crew Duties / ETOPS Dispatch Release
src.quote: A new Pre-Departure Check and amended Dispatch Release are required after the valid time (release expiration), which is four hours after the scheduled departure time.
src.note: 'ETOPS NA' on the release indicates the aircraft is not ETOPS capable; the 'EQUIP ETOPS' line is not an indication of ETOPS status.

q: When does the aircraft reach the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP), and how is the EXP distance related?
a: The EEP is reached when the aircraft is 60 minutes from the adequate airport (at OEI cruise speed, standard conditions, still air). The EXP represents the same 60-minute distance and results in the same fixed distance as the EEP.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.3 — ETOPS Entry/Exit Point/Equal Time Point
src.quote: reaches the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) when it is 60 minutes from the adequate airport
src.note: Flight Crew and Dispatch must use the same adequate airports to define EEP and EXP, and those airports must be listed on the Dispatch Release.

q: Do ETOPS regulations add fuel requirements once in flight, and what does arriving at the CP/ETP below critical fuel actually require?
a: No; ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight. Arriving at the CP/ETP at or above critical fuel is only a dispatch requirement, so there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above arrival requirements.

src.quote: ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight.
src.note: Fuel monitoring remains critical given the potential for a long diversion; the Dispatcher may adjust altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to meet the critical fuel requirement.

q: At what altitude and winds does Alaska calculate Equal-Time Points (ETPs), and what is an ETP?
a: ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft. An ETP is a point where the flight time, considering wind, to each of two selected diversion destinations is equal.

src.quote: ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft.
src.note: Because ETPs are wind-affected, a different ETP exists for each altitude; crews should also stay aware of the airport that takes the least time to reach near cruise altitude.

q: Within what timeframe must ETOPS discrepancies such as IFSDs and diversions be reported?
a: Within 96 hours.

src.quote: Within 96 hours, the certificate holder must report IFSDs, diversions/turnbacks for failures/malfunctions/defects
src.note: Reportable events include uncommanded thrust changes, inability to control thrust, fuel loss/imbalance, and any event jeopardizing safe flight and landing; prompt crew reporting helps meet this requirement.

q: Alaska/Hawaiian's 787 is approved for a maximum ETOPS operation of how many minutes?
a: 180 minutes. (Options were 60, 120, 180, 240 — the authorized Maximum Diversion Time is 180.)

src.quote: The Alaska Airlines' authorized MDT is 180 minutes.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt. MEL-deferred items can occasionally cut the MDT to 120 minutes; the release states the MDT the flight was planned on.

q: ETOPS philosophy is 'Preclude and Protect.' Which is true — that Preclude means avoiding a diversion through maintenance/dispatch/pilot planning, that Protect means the analysis of airports, weather, firefighting, passenger handling, landing performance and fuel to the alternate, or all of the above?
a: All of the above. Preclude = keep the diversion from happening (design, testing, maintenance, dispatch and pilot planning); Protect = if it happens anyway, programs (monitored alternates, enhanced comms, enhanced dispatch fuel) carry it out safely.

src.ref: FOM 6.1.3 — ETOPS Philosophy: Preclude and Protect
src.quote: The premise of ETOPS is to preclude a diversion and, if it were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.1.3. Preclude layers: aircraft/propulsion design and testing, maintenance procedures, flight ops procedures. Protect layers: designated alternates monitored throughout the flight, increased communication requirements, enhanced dispatch fuel.

q: True or false: PACOTS are tracks established WEEKLY via a Track Definition Message and NOTAM, with dispatch providing a copy.
a: FALSE. Organized Pacific tracks (PACOTS) are built and published on a DAILY cycle via the Track Definition Message, not weekly. The 'weekly' claim is what makes the statement false.

src.quote: PACOTS tracks are issued on a daily Track Definition Message cycle, not weekly.
src.note: Not covered in FOM ch6 (oceanic track systems live in the oceanic/international chapters). Marked FALSE per the pop quiz key and consistent with eq04 (Central East Pacific tracks change daily). The specific daily-cycle detail is not in the provided ch6.txt; answer FALSE is the load-bearing point.

q: True or false: the tracks between the US West Coast and Hawaii lie within the Central East Pacific (CEP) track system and change daily.
a: FALSE. Per FOM 6.2.1, any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport may be used as an adequate airport provided it is listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports. Rev 125 removed the HA OpSpec B342/C070 sourcing from the definition. West Coast–Hawaii routings use the Central East Pacific (CEP) organized track system, which is republished daily.
ref: Central East Pacific (CEP) track system / AIP

src.quote: West Coast to Hawaii routes lie in the Central East Pacific (CEP) track system and change daily.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt; oceanic-track knowledge. Supports eq03 (organized Pacific tracks are daily, not weekly).

q: Which is true — that over-water operations begin more than 50 NM from the nearest shoreline and require survival equipment under FAR 121.339, that a flag operation is a scheduled flight from a point in the 48 states/AK/HI/territory to a point outside (or between two points both outside), or all of the above?
a: All of the above. Extended over-water begins beyond 50 NM from the nearest shoreline (survival gear per FAR 121.339); a flag operation is the scheduled international/overseas operation described.

src.quote: An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline.
src.note: The 50 NM over-water definition is VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.1.2. FAR 121.339 (over-water survival equipment) and the flag-operation definition (FAR 1.1) are cited from the question; they are not restated in ch6.txt.

q: True or false: RVSM provides 1,000 ft vertical separation from FL290 up to and including FL410, and with failure of any required RVSM equipment the crew must exit RVSM airspace.
a: TRUE. RVSM gives 1,000 ft separation FL290 through FL410; loss of required altimetry/altitude-control equipment must be reported to ATC and the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace.

src.ref: NAT Doc 007 — RVSM / altimetry failure reporting
src.quote: Loss of one or more primary altimetry systems, or failure of all automatic altitude-control systems, must be reported to ATC as soon as practicable.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt (RVSM lives in the oceanic/international chapters). The equipment-failure reporting requirement is supported by NAT Doc 007 as reflected in the NAT HLA reference.

q: Class I navigation — which is true: that it is operation within the service volume of ground-based facilities (VOR/VORTAC/DME/NDB), that it includes flying through MEA gaps using pilotage/DR or GPS, that VOR service range is about 130 NM and NDB about 75 NM, or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: Class I navigation is conducted within the operational service volume of ICAO-standard ground-based navaids, including short gaps flown by pilotage/DR or GPS.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. The VOR ~130 NM / NDB ~75 NM service ranges are navigation-reference values cited from the question, not from ch6.txt.

q: True or false: Class II (ORCN) navigation is operation outside the service volume of ground-based navaids for more than one hour and requires one Long Range Navigation System (GPS or self-contained IRS) and one Long Range Communication System (HF or SATCOM).
a: TRUE.

src.quote: Class II navigation outside ground-navaid service volume requires a Long Range Navigation System (GPS or IRS) and a Long Range Communication System (HF or SATCOM).
src.note: Not in ch6.txt; ch6.txt 6.2.6 points to '7.1.8 – Long Range Communication System (LRCS) Requirements' for LRCS. Supported by the NAT HLA reference (LRCS = HF/SATCOM).

q: To enter ETOPS airspace where PBCS is used you need Communication, Navigation and Surveillance performance. Which is true — NAV = PBN/RNP, Comm = Performance-Based Communication (RCP), Surveillance = Performance-Based Surveillance (RSP), or all of the above?
a: All of the above. PBCS is built on Performance-Based Navigation (RNP), Required Communication Performance (RCP) and Required Surveillance Performance (RSP).

src.quote: PBCS tracks require Performance-Based Navigation (RNP), Required Communication Performance (RCP) and Required Surveillance Performance (RSP).
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. Supported by the ETOPS review material (PBCS tracks: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, RSP180).

q: True or false: RNP operations carry time limits per OpSpec B036, with specific requirements for specific aircraft types, and MEL issues can affect those time limits.
a: TRUE.

src.quote: OpSpec B036: unlimited with GPS updating, 18 hours with inertial position updating.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. VERIFIED against the NAT HLA reference, which cites OpSpec B036 (unlimited with GPS updating, 18 hours on inertial).

q: True or false: RNP 10 is the minimum navigation requirement for operation in the Central East Pacific.
a: TRUE. RNP 10 (RNAV 10) is the minimum navigation specification for the Central East Pacific.

src.quote: RNP 10 is the minimum navigation requirement for the Central East Pacific.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. Consistent with the NAT HLA reference, which shows RNP 10 as the reduced-capability floor for oceanic entry; RNP 10 is the recognized CEP minimum.

q: True or false: RCP means Required Communication Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 240 seconds depending on the airspace, CPDLC as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment.
a: TRUE (RCP 400 / RCP 240, CPDLC via VHF or SATCOM datalink).

src.quote: Required Communication Performance: RCP 400 or RCP 240 depending on airspace; CPDLC is the application over VHF or SATCOM datalink.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. RCP 240 is the PBCS-track value in the ETOPS review material.

q: True or false: RSP means Required Surveillance Performance, with time requirements of 400 seconds or 180 seconds depending on the airspace, ADS-C as the application and VHF or SATCOM datalink as the equipment.
a: TRUE (RSP 400 / RSP 180, ADS-C via VHF or SATCOM datalink).

src.quote: Required Surveillance Performance: RSP 400 or RSP 180 depending on airspace; ADS-C is the application over VHF or SATCOM datalink.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt. RSP 180 is the PBCS-track value in the ETOPS review material.

q: Operational control — which is true: that the Director of Operations has authority and responsibility for supervision and control of all flight operations, that the FODO can act as DO and authority is delegated to the Controlling Dispatcher and PIC, that the Controlling Dispatcher maintains control through SOCC, or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: The Director of Operations holds authority for control of all flight operations; that authority is exercised jointly by the Controlling Dispatcher (through SOCC) and the PIC.
src.note: Not in ch6.txt (operational control is defined in the general/administrative FOM chapters). ch6.txt 6.3.1 does assign the Dispatcher specific ETOPS duties and 6.4.x pairs the PIC and Dispatcher on diversion decisions.

q: True or false: the Dispatcher is the primary resource in every phase of flight, assists in emergency situations, may declare or initiate emergency procedures, and disseminates emergency information to company personnel and outside agencies.
a: TRUE.

src.quote: The Dispatcher is the primary resource in every phase of flight and shares responsibility with the PIC, including relaying critical information during an ETOPS diversion.
src.note: Not fully in ch6.txt, but ch6.txt 6.3.1 lists the Dispatcher's ETOPS duties (relay weather/NOTAM/field changes, revised ETP and critical fuel) and 6.4.1 pairs the crew 'in concert with Dispatch.'

q: Dispatcher ETOPS duties — which is true: (A) before the EEP the Dispatcher sends current weather/NOTAMs for the ETOPS alternates and requires crew acknowledgement; (B) enroute the Dispatcher monitors the ETOPS alternates for weather/NOTAM/field conditions; (C) enroute the Dispatcher follows fuel consumption and relays significant info and release changes requiring Dispatcher/Captain concurrence; or (D) B and C only?
a: B and C only. The FOM's before-EEP duty is to PROVIDE relevant weather/NOTAM updates for the ETOPS alternates via ACARS/SATCOM/HF — it does not state a crew-acknowledgement requirement — so option A overstates it; the enroute duties in B and C match the FOM.

src.quote: Before EEP: Provide via ACARS, SATCOM, or HF any relevant updates to weather and/or safety of flight NOTAMs for ETOPS alternate airports. Enroute: Evaluate the weather, NOTAMs, and field conditions ... Be aware of any variance in fuel consumption. Relay ... any significant changes ...
src.note: VERIFIED against ch6.txt 6.3.1. The answer excludes A because the FOM before-EEP duty is to 'provide' updates, not to require crew acknowledgement (acknowledgement is tied to verification-flight results and specific message receipts elsewhere).

q: ETOPS 'Preclude'/maintenance — which is true: (A) ETOPS-significant systems are detailed in the manufacturer's configuration/maintenance program; (B) servicing two separate systems, or two of the same ETOPS-significant items, requires an ETOPS-qualified mechanic to sign off (dual-maintenance limitation); (C) ETOPS-significant parts require a specific ETOPS part number; or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: Dual Maintenance Limitations: Restrictions are placed on performing dual maintenance on ETOPS Significant Systems to prevent failures.
src.note: Dual-maintenance limitations and ETOPS-qualified sign-off are VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.1; the ETOPS-significant-systems list (6.5.3) sits in the manufacturer-supplemented ETOPS maintenance program. The specific-ETOPS-part-number detail comes from the ETOPS maintenance program cited in the question and is not spelled out in ch6.txt.

q: True or false: ETOPS in-flight shutdown (IFSD) rate targets come from AC 120-42B, and for a two-engine aircraft operating beyond 120 up to 180 minutes the target IFSD rate must not exceed 0.03 per 1,000 engine-hours.
a: TRUE — per AC 120-42B. For the beyond-120-to-180-minute band the two-engine IFSD rate target is 0.03/1,000 engine-hours.

src.quote: Beyond 120 up to 180 minutes ETOPS: target IFSD rate not to exceed 0.03 per 1,000 engine-hours (per AC 120-42B).
src.note: Per AC 120-42B, the target IFSD rate for the 120-to-180-minute band must not exceed 0.03 per 1000 engine-hours. This is an Advisory Circular figure and is not restated in the FOM chapter text.

q: The ETOPS Pre-Departure Service Check (PDSC) verifies airworthiness by checking which — (A) the condition of the ETOPS-significant systems; (B) overall aircraft status via maintenance records; (C) an interior/exterior inspection including engine and APU oil levels and consumption; or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: Verification of the condition of all ETOPS Significant Systems ... Verification of the overall status of the aircraft by reviewing applicable maintenance records ... An interior and exterior inspection to include a determination of engine and APU oil levels and consumption rates.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4 — these are exactly the three minimum PDC/PDSC elements. Primary responsibility lies with Maintenance; an ETOPS-qualified mechanic must sign the logbook prior to ETOPS operation.

q: The ETOPS PDSC — which is true: (A) it is valid four hours from the Zulu sign-off in the logbook; (B) if the 4-hour limit is exceeded but passenger boarding has begun, the PDSC remains valid but MOC must be notified; (C) if exceeded and boarding has NOT begun, a new PDSC is required; or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the Airworthiness Release block was signed ... If the boarding process started before the four (4) hours lapsed, the flight may continue with the PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. If, at the end of four (4) hours, the flight or aircraft is not ready for departure and boarding has not started, the PDSC is invalidated.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4. MOC monitors the four hours from the PDSC release/sign-off and notifies Maintenance and SOCC/Dispatch if a new PDSC is needed.

q: MEL policy — which is true: (A) prior to pushback/taxi, issues are resolved per the MEL; (B) after pushback and prior to takeoff, issues are resolved per crew placarding; (C) the MEL applies after takeoff; or (D) A and B only?
a: A and B only. The MEL is a pre-takeoff dispatch tool — it does not apply once airborne, so option C is false.

src.quote: Compliance with the MEL is a critical factor in ETOPS operations; MEL relief is a dispatch/pre-takeoff determination and does not apply after takeoff.
src.note: The ETOPS-critical role of the MEL is VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.8; the general rule that the MEL applies before takeoff (not in flight) is standard MEL policy from the FOM's MEL chapter, cited here for the 'A and B only' key.

q: Adequate-airport requirements — which is true: (A) it meets Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF) or is an active/operational military airfield; (B) it accounts for size, surface, obstructions, facilities, public protection, lighting, nav/comm aids and ATC; (C) a turbojet must be able to stop within 60% of the effective runway length from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway; or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: Turbojet aircraft must be able to be stopped within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.1 (all three elements). Note the CAUTION: an adequate airport may still be unsuitable for a diversion (no ARFF, or bad weather).

q: True or false: an airport qualifies as an adequate airport only if it is listed in OpSpec B342 and/or C070.
a: TRUE.

src.quote: Any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport may be used as an adequate airport provided it is listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt: 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 cite Ops Spec B342 and C070 for authorized/adequate airports.

q: For a Dispatcher to list an airport as an ETOPS alternate — which is true: (A) it is an adequate airport listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports; (B) weather reports/forecasts are at or above the ETOPS-alternate minima per OpSpec C055 for the earliest-to-latest landing window; (C) field-condition reports indicate a safe landing can be made; or all of the above?
a: All of the above.

src.quote: The Dispatcher will not list an airport as an ETOPS alternate airport ... unless: the appropriate weather reports or forecasts ... indicate that the weather conditions will be at or above the ETOPS alternate airport minima specified in Ops Spec C055 ... Field condition reports indicate that a safe landing can be made.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.2. The alternate must first be an adequate airport (B342/C070), then meet the C055 weather window and safe-landing field conditions.

q: ARFF for ETOPS alternates — which is true: (A) rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to ICAO Category 4 or higher; (B) firefighting support within a 30-minute response time; or (C) both A and B?
a: Both A and B. Each designated ETOPS alternate needs at least ICAO Category 4 RFFS and meets a 30-minute response time.

src.ref: FOM 6.2.2 — Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Requirements
src.quote: Each designated ETOPS alternate airport must have rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher ... firefighting assistance within a 30-minute response time.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.2.2. The 30-minute response time does NOT mean trucks idle for 30 minutes; it means equipment is available on arrival of the diverting airplane and stays on station as long as needed.

q: Check-airman scenario: You're 8 minutes from the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) on a 787 to Honolulu when Dispatch relays that your designated ETOPS alternate's weather has just dropped below the crew's operating minima and no METAR is coming. What is required, and how would it differ if this happened AFTER the EEP?
a: Before the EEP: you must have a suitable ETOPS alternate to enter the ETOPS area. Coordinate with Dispatch to establish a new ETOPS alternate; if none can be designated (and the existing one is no longer available), a turnback is required before crossing the EEP. After the EEP: a turnback is NOT required just because the alternate is below the crew's operating minima or the runway is unusable — you attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch, which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation, and the PIC and Dispatcher exercise judgment on the safest course.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.5 — In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
src.quote: From after takeoff until approaching the EEP: ... A turnback is required if an ETOPS alternate is no longer available. After the EEP: A turnback is not required if weather at the ETOPS alternate is below the crew's operating minima or the runway is unusable. If required, attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation on planned route.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.3.5. The EEP is the hinge: pre-EEP the alternate must be suitable to enter; post-EEP the crew and Dispatch work the problem in flight rather than automatically turning back.

q: Check-airman scenario: Cruising the CEP between two ETOPS alternates, you pass the fuel-critical Equal-Time Point (ETP) and a few minutes later get a single-engine event. Which airport, what speed, and what's the governing rule?
a: Divert to the nearest SUITABLE airport in the Captain's judgment (14 CFR 121.565). By definition of the ETP, once you're past it the airport ahead now takes the least time, so it is generally the diversion field. Fly the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed, M.84/290 KIAS, which is the fueled/planned diversion speed; the Captain may deviate only after assessing the emergency and considering fuel remaining. Note the ETP is a wind-based planning point (Alaska computes ETPs at 10,000 ft) and the flight-planning system does not account for the time/fuel to make the 180° turn near the ETP.

src.quote: 14 CFR 121.565 requires the Captain of a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative to land at the nearest suitable airport where, in the Captain's judgment after considering all relevant factors, a safe landing can be made.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.4.2 (nearest suitable), 6.4.5 (OEI cruise speed = the planned diversion speed; Captain may deviate after assessing emergency and fuel), 6.3.7 (ETP is per-altitude, wind-affected, computed at 10,000 ft), and 6.4.1 (turn time/fuel near a fuel-critical ETP is not modeled by the flight-planning system).

q: Check-airman scenario: Maintenance signs the ETOPS PDSC at 0400Z. A gate hold pushes departure late. Walk through what happens if boarding began at 0730Z versus if, at 0800Z, boarding still hasn't started.
a: The PDSC Airworthiness Release is valid four hours from the sign-off time (0400Z to 0800Z). If boarding began before the four hours lapsed (0730Z is inside the window), the flight may continue on the existing PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. If, at the end of the four hours (0800Z), the aircraft isn't ready and boarding has NOT started, the PDSC is invalidated and a new PDSC is required. MOC monitors the four-hour clock and notifies Maintenance and SOCC/Dispatch if a new PDSC is needed. Separately, if the crew suspects a maintenance action invalidated the PDSC, they contact MOC via Dispatch.

src.quote: An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the Airworthiness Release block was signed ... If the boarding process started before the four (4) hours lapsed, the flight may continue with the PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4. Do not confuse this maintenance PDSC 4-hour clock (from logbook sign-off) with the Dispatch Release/PDC validity, which runs four hours from the scheduled departure time (6.3.2 / 6.5.4).

q: Check-airman scenario: Still short of the EEP, your fuel readout suggests estimated fuel on board at the CP/ETP will come in below the critical-fuel-scenario figure on the release. Are you required to divert before the critical point?
a: No. Arriving at the CP/ETP with fuel on board at or above the critical fuel scenario is only a DISPATCH requirement — ETOPS regulations add no additional fuel requirement once in flight. If it appears estimated FOB at the CP/ETP will be low, there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above the arrival requirements. The Dispatcher should evaluate changes to altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to try to meet the flight plan's critical fuel requirement, though it may not always be possible. Keep monitoring fuel closely given the potential for a long diversion.

The critical fuel is planned from the CP/ETP to the diversion airport using the worst of three scenarios (both engines to 10,000 ft; one engine to best single-engine altitude; one engine to 10,000 ft) plus a 1,500 ft / 15-minute hold / approach-and-land allowance, winds increased 5% (6.2.5).
